correctness.rationale: The published unique-index length theorem fixes the exact object and removes only the initial empty prefix. A period matrix gives an order-two Cayley–Hamilton recurrence with explicitly computed two initial values in each phase; its exact solution is the displayed two-eigenvalue expression. Positive Perron coefficients order the within-period thresholds and give a strict interperiod wrap gap. The second eigenvalue has modulus below one, so the actual integer thresholds are eventually nearest-integer roundings of their Perron terms and differ from ideal thresholds at O(1) integers per exponentially growing period. Consequently the centered count equals a finite-branch staircase except at O(log X) cutoffs. Harmonic integration gives the uniform logarithmic phase and the stated pushforward density; geometric-annulus integration gives the ordinary phase-conditioned density, and differentiation proves that its means vary. Branch endpoint limits prove the exact liminf and limsup. Literal-word palindromic closure was independently reconstructed for 12 directives, with 360,000 integer-count comparisons, 630 spectral comparisons and three ordinary-phase empirical mean checks. These finite computations are consistency checks, not a substitute for the proof.

value.rationale: The 2026 research explicitly identifies a logarithmic counting asymptotic with an irreducibly oscillating bounded error. Determining an entire exact and computable asymptotic error distribution, the phase-dependent ordinary-sampling family (which has no single mean limit), the sharp two-sided oscillation endpoints, and eventual Perron-term integer rounding quantifies this natural unresolved second-order phenomenon in every periodic-directive Sturmian word. It supplies the full statistical and structural behavior of the count’s residual rather than a textbook first-order rephrasing. In particular, the Fibonacci word has uniform harmonic error but constant-two directives produce a nonuniform piecewise density; that distinction is not implied by knowing only the logarithmic coefficient or an O(1) error.
